faqs.question: What is an online proposal for a girlfriend?
faqs.answer: It is a single web page you build from a template and send as a link — your photos, your story and the question she answers by tapping. She opens it in a browser from your chat; there is nothing to download.

faqs.question: How long should the page be if she is reading it on her phone?
faqs.answer: Budget seconds rather than paragraphs. In a 16-subject mobile reading study, a scrolling layout was read at 178.1 words per minute, so roughly 180 to 270 words gets you 60 to 90 seconds of reading before the question.

faqs.question: What should she see before she scrolls?
faqs.answer: Her name, one photo and the question itself. Platform-wide, 48.4% of views of shared SubhSandesh pages happen on a phone, so the first screen is the only part of the page you can count on her seeing.

faqs.question: Should I use the marry-me template or the 'I love you' page?
faqs.answer: If you mean the marriage question, use the Will You Marry Me scrapbook. If you mean asking her to be your girlfriend — which is what "propose" usually means in Indian usage — the I love you page fits better; it is the second most-created page type on the platform at 1,173 pages, 23.2%.

faqs.question: Does it matter that she might open it while she is moving?
faqs.answer: It does. In a study of 30 people reading on a phone, comprehension scores fell to 34.7% while walking a course with pedestrian traffic against 51.7% sitting down. Build the page so she can leave it and come back without restarting, and keep the ask short enough to survive a distracted read.

faqs.question: Should I password-protect the proposal page?
faqs.answer: Lock it if her chat is shared or her phone gets passed around; 38.7% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it, measured platform-wide across all 20 page types. Just remember the password box then becomes the first thing she sees, so send the password in the same message.

faqs.question: How many photos should go on the page?
faqs.answer: Few enough that the question is not pushed off the first screen. One photo above the fold and a small handful below it beats a gallery she has to swipe through before she learns what you are asking.

faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027?
faqs.answer: Monday 8 February 2027. It is the second day of Valentine week, after Rose Day on Sunday 7 February, and the week ends with Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February 2027.

faqs.question: Is sending a link a worse way to propose than saying it out loud?
faqs.answer: If she is in the same room, yes — go and say it. A page is for crossing distance or for giving her something she can reopen; it is not a substitute for being present when you could be.

faqs.question: What if she opens it somewhere she cannot react?
faqs.answer: That is the main risk of a link: an office desk or a lecture turns your one first time into a hurried one-word reply. Send it when you know she has five quiet minutes rather than when you happen to finish building it.

faqs.question: Does an online proposal work for a long-distance relationship?
faqs.answer: It is the case a link is actually built for, since the page arrives the moment you send it. The same phone constraints apply, and a time-zone gap makes the first-screen rule matter more, not less.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Online Proposal for Girlfriend: Built for a Phone Screen

An online proposal for girlfriend is a page you build and send her as a link, and she will open it on a phone, one-handed, somewhere you did not choose. Platform-wide across the 20 page types on SubhSandesh, 48.4% of views arrive on a phone — 27,185 of 56,152 views, measured 2026-09-23 — and 91.2% of the 5,061 pages started since 2026-03-12 are published and shared. Neither figure is measured on proposal pages; no proposal-specific number exists here.

So this page is not a list of what to put on yours. It is the set of limits a phone screen puts on the ask: what has to be visible before she scrolls, how many words she will realistically get through, and what to cut so the question survives a crowded bus.

## What an online proposal page is, and what it is not

It is one web page, built from a template, that carries your photos and your story and ends in a question she answers by tapping. It is not an app and not a file she downloads; it opens in whatever browser her chat app hands the link to.

Two different questions get called a proposal. One is "will you marry me". The other, which in Indian usage is what "propose" usually means, is "will you be my girlfriend" — the asking, not the wedding.

The template you pick should match the question, and the shape of the page changes with it.

The scale here is platform-wide, not proposal-specific: 5,061 pages across 20 page types since 2026-03-12, at an average of 11.1 views per page.

## She reads it on a phone, in the middle of something else

The phone is not a small desktop. It is a screen held in a moving hand in a room you cannot see, and that changes what a page can ask of her.

Movement alone costs her something. In a Carleton University study, [30 volunteers read passages on a phone while walking a course with pedestrian traffic](https://carleton.scholaris.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/561a70c5-23d3-4343-afa1-374d08b74ebd/content) and scored 34.7% on the comprehension test, against 51.7% for the same passages read sitting down (F(1,27) = 5.19, p = 0.031) — and the auto-scrolling interface built to fix that did not close the gap.

There is also a cost to being interrupted at all. In a [controlled experiment with 48 participants who were interrupted every two minutes](https://www.ics.uci.edu/~gmark/chi08-mark.pdf), people finished the work faster, not slower — but reported significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. Those were office tasks, not love letters, so read it as a warning rather than a measurement of your girlfriend: an interruption always takes something out of the reader, and a page that only works if she reads it start to finish in one sitting is a page you have made fragile.

## Four limits a phone screen puts on your proposal page

Each limit below states the constraint, the evidence behind it, what to do about it, and what the fix costs you. All four follow from the same platform-wide fact — 48.4% of 56,152 views are phone views — and from two reading studies run on phones and screens.

### 1. The first screen carries the ask

**The limit.** Whatever sits above her first scroll is the only part you can count on.

**The evidence.** Platform-wide, 48.4% of the 56,152 recorded views are phone views, so for roughly half your audience of one, "the page" means a screen about the size of a postcard.

**What to do.** Put her name, one photo and the question itself in that first screen. The story goes below it.

**The tradeoff.** You lose the slow reveal. If the build-up is the point, you are choosing drama over certainty, and you should know that is the trade.

### 2. Write to a word budget, not a word count

**The limit.** Length is measured in her seconds, not your paragraphs.

**The evidence.** In a [mobile-phone reading study of 16 subjects](http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:169379/FULLTEXT01.pdf), text presented a screen at a time was read at 217.7 words per minute against 178.1 for a scrolling layout, with no significant difference in comprehension. At 178 words per minute, 200 words is about 67 seconds. Chopping the text smaller does not buy you more: in an [eye-tracking study of on-screen reading formats](https://bop.unibe.ch/JEMR/article/download/2336/3532/8560), format significantly changed fixation duration (F3,60 = 22.102, p < .001) while measured reading speeds stayed between 128 and 156 words per minute.

**What to do.** Budget 60 to 90 seconds of reading — roughly 180 to 270 words — before the question, and cut to fit.

**The tradeoff.** Real detail gets deleted. Keep the one memory only the two of you have; drop the three that merely prove you were paying attention.

### 3. Build it to survive one interruption

**The limit.** She will be pulled away mid-page at least once, and she should not have to restart.

**The evidence.** The same 48-participant interruption experiment found people compensating by working faster under measurably higher stress; the disruption is real even when the output looks fine.

**What to do.** Let every section stand on its own, and never gate the question behind an animation she has to sit through or a timer that resets.

**The tradeoff.** Self-contained sections read as slightly less cinematic. That is a fair price for a page she can rejoin at a red light.

### 4. If you lock it, the lock is the first screen

**The limit.** A password moves the ask one screen further away.

**The evidence.** Platform-wide, 38.7% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it — 1,961 of 5,061 pages, across all 20 types.

**What to do.** Lock it if the chat is shared or the phone gets passed around, and send the password in the same message so she is not hunting for it on a moving bus.

**The tradeoff.** You trade the first moment for privacy. If nobody else touches her phone, you are spending the best screen you have on a door.

## Which page she needs: marry me, be mine, or one date

The template should match the question, and for a lot of this traffic the marriage template is simply the wrong door. The table compares the four routes by what they actually ask, with creation figures measured platform-wide across all 20 page types on 2026-09-23.

| Template | What it asks her | Created, platform-wide (of 5,061 pages) | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| [I love you page](/love-gf) | Be mine — the asking, not the wedding | 1,173 pages, 23.2%; most-viewed type at 16,902 views, 30.1% | "Propose" means asking her to be your girlfriend |
| [Will You Marry Me proposal scrapbook](/proposal) | Will you marry me | Not separately measurable — no proposal-specific read exists | You mean the marriage question, and she is expecting the conversation |
| [apology dashboard](/apology-dashboard) | Sorry first, then the ask | 1,347 pages, 26.6% — the most-created type on the platform | You are asking after a fight, or asking again after a no |
| [date invitation page](/date-invitation) | Come on one date | Outside the top five created types | She has not said yes to anything yet |

The honest reading of that table: the marriage scrapbook is the page people picture and often not the page they need. The "I love you" page is the second most-created type on the platform and the most-viewed one, and it is built for the smaller, earlier question — which is the question most people mean when they say they want to propose.

None of those shares are proposal-page rates. They are counts of what everyone on the platform builds, romantic and otherwise, and a proposal page's own numbers are not something we can read today.

## When a phone page is the wrong way to ask

If she is in the next room, close the laptop and go and say it. A link is a way to cross distance, and there is no distance to cross.

It is also the wrong format if she will be somewhere she cannot react — an office desk with people behind her, a lecture, a family dinner. The page will be read in a hurry and answered in a word, and you will have spent your one first time on a bad five minutes.

And a page is not a rescue. Median time from first save to last edit is 2.4 hours, sampled on the apology dashboard with n=1,348 — people come back and rewrite this kind of page rather than firing it off, which is a hint about how much a careless one is worth.

One more limit worth naming: everything on this page about how people read comes from studies of reading in general, not from anyone reading a proposal. A page from someone she loves gets attention a news article never will. The phone constraints still apply; the indifference does not.

## Sources

- Gustav Öquist, *Evaluating Readability on Mobile Devices* (Uppsala University / Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis, 2006) — [paging read at 217.7 WPM against 178.1 WPM for scrolling on a mobile phone, n=16](http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:169379/FULLTEXT01.pdf)
- Selina Sharmin, Oleg Špakov and Kari-Jouko Räihä, "The Effect of Different Text Presentation Formats on Eye Movement Metrics in Reading", *Journal of Eye Movement Research* 5(3):3, 2012 — [presentation format significantly changed fixation duration (F3,60 = 22.102, p < .001) while measured reading speeds stayed between 128 and 156 WPM](https://bop.unibe.ch/JEMR/article/download/2336/3532/8560)
- Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, "The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress", CHI 2008 — [48 participants interrupted every two minutes worked faster but reported significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort](https://www.ics.uci.edu/~gmark/chi08-mark.pdf)
- Andrew Hamel, *An Adaptive User Interface for Walking While Reading on a Mobile Device* (Carleton University, 2017) — [30 participants scored 34.7% on a reading comprehension test while walking a course with pedestrian traffic, against 51.7% sitting, F(1,27) = 5.19, p = 0.031](https://carleton.scholaris.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/561a70c5-23d3-4343-afa1-374d08b74ebd/content)

auditReport.honestAssessment: The one substantive reason to cite this over anything else on the query is that it is the only page in the cluster about the conditions the proposal is read in rather than what goes on it: a measured word budget (178.1 WPM scrolling against 217.7 paging on a phone, n=16), a first-screen rule carried by the platform-wide 48.4% phone-view share that no competitor can publish, and an interruption rule from a 48-participant experiment. All four of its sources were read in full and none of them appears anywhere else in this batch. Against that, the cannibalisation risk is real and named in the research brief: a wave-2 sibling, will-you-be-my-girlfriend-proposal-page-online, already describes the first screen and the chat preview from the recipient's side, and the two pages touch at that edge even though this one reasons from reading speeds rather than from what to write. The SERP behind this post was not properly measured — one US-served result set of titles and snippets, no page fetched — so nothing here describes an incumbent, and the sibling posts show subhsandesh.in ranking nowhere in the 11 India-served SERPs measured on 2026-09-16 for this cluster. With 46 proposal articles already live on the domain plus 42 in waves 1 and 2, this page competes with its own corpus as much as with anyone else's, and a searcher who wants a builder rather than an argument will bounce. Ranking is not predicted.

structuralLimitations: No proposal-specific data exists. The read-only probe of the `proposalpages` collection is refused by this machine's production-read policy, so every SubhSandesh figure in the post is labelled in body prose as platform-wide across 20 page types, or as sampled on the named template (the 2.4-hour edit gap, sampled on /apology-dashboard, n=1,348).

The pricing block in content/facts.md is empty for the third batch running, so the post states no price, no tier and no cost claim of any kind — including the detail a reader in this market most wants before choosing a tool.

Phase 1 is inherited and partial. One US-served WebSearch result set was seen on 2026-09-23 as titles and snippets; no competitor page was fetched and this exact keyword is absent from the 11 India-served SERPs measured on 2026-09-16, so no current competitor position or claim is described anywhere in the post.

The source set was changed late for a cap reason, not an editorial one: a Behavioral Sciences (MDPI) eye-tracking study was dropped after the batch verifier showed MDPI at four posts once DOIs resolve, over the three-post publisher cap, and replaced with a Carleton University thesis that was read in full.
All four studies measure reading in general, not anyone reading a proposal page from a partner. The post says so in body prose rather than letting the numbers imply a finding about proposal pages.
